summary: Help 10–13 year-olds read distance-time graphs by treating the LINE as an abstract record of a distance–time relationship, not a picture of terrain. The decisive goal is overcoming the graph-as-picture misconception (upward slope = 'walking up a hill') and slope-height confusion (judging speed by how high the line is rather than how steep). Learners should map each line segment to a motion (moving away, stopped, returning, fast vs slow), read speed from the gradient (flat = stationary, steeper = faster; when the vertical axis shows distance from the start, a downward slope = returning), translate both directions between a written journey and a graph, and compute a segment's average speed as distance ÷ time. A live motion-and-graph coupling is the primary vehicle; card-matching, annotated reference graphs, and embodied walk-the-graph activities are complementary.
misconceptions: Graph-as-picture (iconic confusion): reading the line as a literal picture of terrain — e.g. an upward slope means 'walking up a hill' (Clement 1985; IOP Spark; persists to college level).
Slope-height confusion: judging speed from a point's height on the axis instead of the line's gradient (McDermott et al.; ~half of science students err).
Reading a distance or time value off the graph and calling it the speed — forgetting speed needs BOTH distance and time (Oak National Academy).
Assuming the line must start at the origin (0,0) even when the object begins at a distance from the reference point.
Drawing physically impossible graphs — vertical lines (infinite speed) or lines going 'backwards' in time.
Confusing a distance-time graph with a speed-time/velocity-time graph and interpreting features accordingly.

activities.title: Two-pane motion grapher: watch the line draw itself
steps: In DRIVE mode, send a cart along a straight track with distance markers and a clock, and watch a distance-time graph plot live beneath it in lockstep.
Stop the cart and observe the line go flat; send the cart back toward the start and observe the line slope downward (the graph plots the cart's distance from the start).
Make the cart go fast and then slow, and compare how the line's steepness changes with a live 'speed = gradient' readout.
In BUILD mode, drag a graph segment steeper, predict what the cart will do, then watch: the cart zooms faster along the FLAT track rather than 'climbing'.
Explore a deliberately 'hill-shaped' journey scene and explain why the line is still just a record of distance over time, not a picture of a hill.
activities.insight: The line is a record of the relationship between distance and time; its steepness means speed, not terrain. Making the line steeper makes the object faster — it does not make the object climb.

activities.title: Walk the graph (embodied journey)
steps: Walk a journey along a marked distance line on the floor against a timer while classmates predict the shape of the resulting graph.
Pause partway (stand still) and discuss what the line does during that pause.
Walk back toward the start and note how the graph's slope changes direction (it slopes downward because the graph shows distance from the start).
Compare a fast walk and a slow walk and connect the difference to the steepness of the segments.
activities.insight: Grounding the abstraction in lived motion builds the motion→line link: stopping produces a flat section, returning toward the start produces a downward slope (when distance is measured from the start), and faster walking produces a steeper line.

activities.title: Read the axes and narrate each stage
steps: Before interpreting any feature, state what the vertical axis measures, what the horizontal axis measures, and what the origin represents.
Describe, stage by stage, what is happening on a given graph — moving away, stopped, returning, fast or slow.
Identify the fastest section by finding the STEEPEST segment (greatest gradient), not the highest point.
Calculate the average speed of one straight segment as distance ÷ time for that segment, using the axis scales.
activities.insight: Speed is read from the gradient of a segment (distance ÷ time), while the horizontal flat section means stationary; the highest point is not necessarily the fastest.

activities.title: Translate both ways: match and sketch
steps: Match journey descriptions (e.g. 'she stopped for lunch, then hurried home') to the correct graph segments or whole graphs, in small groups.
Sketch a distance-time graph from a written journey that includes stops and speed changes, including a return to the start.
Sketch the graph for a cyclist who sets off slowly and speeds up smoothly — a curve that starts shallow and gets steeper (concave up), not a straight line and not a hill-shaped picture.
Order four runners by speed by comparing the gradients of their lines.
Point to a place on your own sketch where the object is stopped and explain how the graph shows it.
activities.insight: Fluent interpretation means translating in both directions between a written journey and the graph, treating the graph as an abstract distance-time relationship rather than a literal picture of the route.

activities.title: Annotated reference graph (recap)
steps: Use a pre-drawn, annotated distance-time graph (distance measured from the start) where each segment is labelled: flat = stationary, steep = fast, downward slope = returning toward the start.
Tap or lift a flap on the flat part to confirm 'stopped', and on the steep part to confirm 'fastest — look at the gradient'.
Use it as a quick recap or reference card when interpreting new graphs.
activities.insight: A clean labelled reference consolidates the segment-to-motion vocabulary once the motion→line link has been built elsewhere.

checkQuestion: Here is a distance-time graph of a cyclist's trip: it rises steeply, then flattens into a horizontal line, then rises gently. Point to the part where the cyclist is going FASTEST, and tell me what the flat horizontal part means. Then sketch the graph for a cyclist who sets off slowly and speeds up smoothly.
checkAnswer: Fastest is the STEEPEST section (greatest gradient) — the first steep rise — not the highest point. The horizontal flat part means the cyclist is STOPPED (distance not changing while time passes), not 'riding on flat ground'. The 'slowly then speeding up' sketch is a curve that starts shallow and gets steeper (concave up), not a straight line and not a hill-shaped picture.
